newsitem.title: UK: Slow, painful steps in N. Ireland's peace process.
newsitem.headline: Slow, painful steps in N. Ireland's peace process.

text.p: The British government was expected to lose a key vote on disarming guerrilla groups in Northern Ireland peace talks on Wednesday.

Pro-British Protestant politicians angered at the terms of last weekend's Irish Republican Army (IRA) ceasefire were expected to block approval of a deal under which the guerrillas would not have to disarm before their allies joined the talks.
The IRA ceasefire will admit Sinn Fein, the guerrillas' political wing, to the peace talks in September if the truce is deemed genuine by Britain.
But unionists want Sinn Fein to secure the handover of IRA arms to prove a commitment to democracy as the sole means of achieving its goal of an end to British rule of the province.
The vote at multi-party talks was part of Anglo-Irish efforts to bring peace to the province that began in 1993. Here is a chronology of key events since then:

December - Northern Ireland peace process launched with the Anglo-Irish Downing Street Declaration which said that Britain would not block an end to British rule if a majority wanted it and offered Sinn Fein a seat at peace talks if violence ended.
Sept 1 - IRA starts ceasefire.
Oct 14 - Pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas start truce.
Dec 9 - British officials hold first open meeting with Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA, in more than 70 years.
February 22 - "Framework Document" published by the British and Irish governments. Forms basis of negotiations on a political settlement for Northern Ireland.
March 22 - British minister holds first talks with Protestant political parties linked to loyalist guerrillas.
May 10 - Britain ends 23-year ban on ministerial talks with Sinn Fein.
June 18 - Sinn Fein breaks off exploratory peace talks with Britain, angered at British attitude to IRA arms.
Sept 5 - Ireland abruptly postpones summit talks with Britain, refusing to link future all-party peace talks to London's insistence that IRA guerrillas disarm.
Sept 19 - Spokesmen for loyalist gunmen hold their first peace talks with the Irish government.
Nov 28 - London and Dublin announce "twin-track" process setting end of February 1996 for start of all-party talks and announcing commission to study arms issue.
Nov 30 - U.S President Bill Clinton visits Northern Ireland.
Dec 15 - International commission under former U.S. senator George Mitchell tries to resolve weapons row.
Dec 19 - Sinn Fein holds first ministerial talks with Britain.
Jan 24 - Mitchell proposes talks alongside phased surrender of guerrilla weapons. Instead, British Prime Minister John Major proposes elections in Northern Ireland to pave way for talks.
Feb 9 - IRA goes back to war, setting off a huge bomb in London's Docklands commercial and residential district in the east end, killing two people.
Feb 28 - Major and Irish Prime Minister John Bruton revive peace process and announce June 10 date for all-party talks. They say Sinn Fein will be excluded unless the IRA ceasefire restarts.
May 30 - Elections in Northern Ireland for new political Forum see Sinn Fein increase share of vote to 15 percent.
June 10 - Multi-party talks on the future of Northern Ireland begin in Belfast, but Sinn Fein is excluded.

May 1 - Sinn Fein wins 16 percent of the Northern Irish vote in Britain's May 1 general election and returns party president Gerry Adams and his chief negotiatior, Martin McGuinness, to the British parliament. Neither man takes up his seat.
May 21 - Britain's new Labour government ends 16-month ban on contacts with Sinn Fein and holds talks.
June 25 - Blair unveils new proposals including an independent commission to oversee the scrapping of guerrilla arms in parallel with talks on a political settlement.
July 14 - Britain acknowledges official contacts with Sinn Fein to clarify conditions for the group's eventual admission to peace talks.
July 15 - Northern Ireland peace talks resume in Belfast with Unionists angered by British contacts with Sinn Fein.
July 18 - Sinn Fein asks IRA to restore truce, saying Britain has removed some obstacles to negotiations.
July 19 - IRA announces "unequivocal" ceasefire to start at noon ono Sunday July 20.
July 21 - Small UK Unionist Party quits peace talks. Unionist politicians say Sinn Fein should not be allowed into talks without IRA commitment to hand in its arms.
July 22 - Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionist Party says it will quit talks as British government acknowledges it will lose proposal on arms decomissioning.
Unionist parties make clear they will block an Anglo-Irish proposal which sees decommissioning of guerrilla arms tackled by subcommittee in parallel with political negotiations.
